projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Eugene R. Painter was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Eugene R. Painter. Mr. Painter served in the U.S. Navy and with the Seabees. Gene served on the Battleship Arizona before the war and in North Africa with the Seabees. His highest rank was Carpenter's Mate First Class. I am Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Painter's home in Shardon, Ohio, on October 24th, 2002. Gene was 88 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me about when you went into the Navy, then. What year was that? How old were you?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I've got to get out--something out here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Basically, retell what you just told me a couple of minutes ago.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Well, I joined the--I joined the regular Navy--I graduated from high school in 1932 and there wasn't a job. That was the Depression. So I thought I could get into the--I took the test to West Point, and the congressman's neighbor got appointed. And then the American Legion folks in Chardon set it up and I--and I got set up and went into the regular Navy and--to go to _________ school for Annapolis. I went up--I went through training in Great Lakes. And they closed Great Lakes Training Station, the only time in history, and they shipped us to San Diego. I finished my training there and went aboard the Battleship Arizona, I think it was in July of 1933. I was in the Fourth Division, which is the deck division. And I had been in there about a year and the gentleman in charge of the Number Two Catapult needed a striker, and he asked me would I take the job, and I was tickled to death to. So I--I began working on the catapult. And you know, the battleships carried planes for observation. And--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What does a striker do?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I'm just a helper.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. It's just the name for the helper?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Just a helper.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Yeah. Striker. Then--I'd been on there about a year and I had about two years in the regular Navy, and this gentleman I was working for transferred from the regular Navy into Naval aviation. And I was a Seaman First Class. And the--the division officer said, "Painter, if--if the commander will okay it, I'm going to put you in charge. You should be a Gunner's Mate Third." But--"You've got the experience and the know-how." So he said--a week or so later, he come up and he said, "Painter, the commander said, 'Go ahead, take over.'" Those days, advancement in the regular Navy was by exam. And as soon as I was eligible, I took the exam for Gunner's Mate Third. And, of course, I made it. And then I served the rest of my term as the--in charge of the catapult. And when we went to--to our battle stations--after the planes were in the air, I--I was in the upper chamber of the Number Four Turret, which were 14-inch guns. And when I first went aboard, I started in the magazines, and then on the shell deck, and worked my way up to the--to the upper chambers. And the--the division officer had me trained as a gun captain, assistant gun captain, primerman, shellman, and rammerman. So I could relieve--in case of emergency, I could relieve anybody. And that's what I did until I left. The--in the short-range shooting in 1935. We scored a great score at--and we got the Navy "E." Do you know what that is?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Explain that again.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Navy "E," efficiency. So I finished out my term. And when I was--I had about two weeks to go and--and I got a telegram from my dad. My mother was in the hospital. They didn't expect her to live. And I went right to my division officer and I said, "You know, I'm going to be discharged in two weeks. Is there any chance that you can get me discharged now so I can go home and..." He said, "You give me an hour to talk to the commander." And within an hour he come back with my discharge papers and said, "Good luck to you and please come back. We would like to have you stay in the Navy." And I said, "Well, I--I'm not that interested." So anyway, I come home. And when my mother--my dad said to me, "You know, son, when Mom saw you, she started getting better immediately." So Mom got back on her feet. And that was the first session in the good old U.S. Navy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was life on board the battleship like?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Well, it was very regulated. And you got out of the regular Navy exactly what you put in it. I--I went up the ladder as fast as--as it was possible. As soon as I was eligible, I took a test and I went up. When I went aboard, I was an apprentice seaman making $17 a month, and then they increased that to $21 a month just before I made Seaman Second Class and--and that went up gradually to 36 bucks, 54. And as a Gunner's Mate Third Class, I was making 66 bucks a month. And I had--I had by then determined I was going to marry this lady that I am now living with. And so we started a saving's account, joint. We weren't--we weren't even married yet. And so when I got out of the Navy, we set the date for our wedding and--and I went out and I bought a brand-new Chevrolet Coup for 600 bucks. And--anyway, on September the 3rd, 1937, her and I--we got married. Couldn't afford a wedding or couldn't afford a--because there wasn't any money, you know. We went to her minister and we had a couple that had been our friends ever since high school days. They stood up with us. We got married, went out for dinner, and took a little trip to New York State. It was raining all the time, so we came home and called it quits. And we rented a one-room apartment in--up in east Cleveland, at the corner of Ivanhoe Road and Route 20. And we stayed there one year. And I went into the building business with my dad. And then I bought four lots on Opelika Drive in Chesterland, and I started building a new house. And I got that baby built and we moved into it not finished. And that's when I went into the Seabees.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Getting back to the Arizona: Was the home port San Diego for the Arizona when you went in?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the home port?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: San Pedro. Long Beach, San Pedro.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: And we--I--I came from the country. And when I went out to the West Coast, you know, I had to grow up. You know, they talk about homos. Well, the people in the--in this country don't understand the homos. You didn't dare walk down--they had a boardwalk in--in Long Beach. You walked down there and it would be six of them guys approach ya. What a different world, you know. So I came home. I belong to the Arizona Reunion Group. I don't go because it's--they meet in Tucsan the first week of December every year. And since I've been in it, my health has been lousy and I haven't got--I have a guy that wants badly to take me out there. But I'm operating on a pacemaker and all of that stuff, and--the health hasn't been good, so...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were back home working for what? About four years before the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I came home in '37, they hit it in '41. And that was on December the 7th, '41. Mom and I were--we were just getting ready to move into our new house, and I said, "I'm going to go and volunteer." I said, "We don't have any children." And she said, "Whatever you decide to do, that's fine with me." So early in January '42--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember specifically, have memories of that day, of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Sure do. It was a Sunday.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I was building my house. And--and my mother-in-law and father-in-law came early every Sunday morning because my father-in-law was helping me. And he come that morning and--and they knocked on the door, and he said, "Did you hear what happened recently?" I said, "What are"--I never turned on a TV or radio in the morning, you know. He said, "Well, they hit Pearl Harbor." I said, "They did?" "Yeah." He says, "I think your old home is down at the bottom of the--of Pearl Harbor." I said, "Gee, that's terrible." So then we turned on the--on the radio and listened to what was going on. And as you know, it was all confused. The--the--and as I analyze this--and I'm going to tell you things that maybe you ain't going to like to hear. As I analyze that, I think President Roosevelt sacrificed Pearl Harbor to get into World War II. That's my personal opinion. I have a lot of people that think the same as I do.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why do you think that?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Because we needed a reason to get into the--to World War II. And as you well know, if you've heard people talk, they had a lot of--of information leading to the facts that the Japs were considering to do this. But we didn't do anything about defense. A little more about the battleship. When they opened Pearl Harbor in the early '30s, we were the third battleship to go in and anchor in Pearl Harbor, and I was in and out of there many times before I left the battleship. It was kind of like a second home down there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you realized the Arizona had been destroyed?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Well, I was very sad, of course. I was proud of my time on the Arizona, and I--and--and you can tell that that type of living for a young guy--you get your priorities in life straightened out. And--so by the time I had been on there a couple of years, I knew exactly where I wanted to go when I got out and what I wanted to do. And--and my father was in the construction business, and I had, as a young man, worked with him. And so I had a little background in it. And when I came home, I--I started working for my dad. And then we were--you know, there was big changes taking place in the construction business those days. And I finally said to Dad, I said, "Dad, the way things are going," I said, "I think I ought to be your partner instead of working for you." And he said, "Okay, son." So we formed the company called RH Painter & Son General Contractors. And I stuck right with it until Pearl Harbor. I went back in the service.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How soon after Pearl Harbor did you sign up?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Did I sign up?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, for the Seabees.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: They hit the--they hit Pearl Harbor in December, I signed up in January, and I was called in in April. And we trained at Camp Little Something or Other in Virginia. And I went--I had to go through military training again, just like I did four years prior--or earlier. And then out of there we--we went to Davisville, Rhode Island, and--and we were--being in construction, we were putting up quansa huts and everything. We were working, you know, building the base, plus doing a little training. And then they shipped us to Gulf Port, Mississippi. We were started for the South Pacific. We got down to Gulf Port. And I don't know what happened and we were there just two weeks and they loaded us on a train and shipped us back to Davisville. Then--let's see. Then--well, just 60 years ago right now, from Davisville they sent us to Long Island, New York. We were housed in a hotel there. And on the--on the last day of the month of October, they put us aboard the U.S.S. Hermitage, which is--was an Italian ship that the Navy took over down in the Panama, and it was a troop transport. And we left New Jersey on the first day of November, 1942. And, of course, it was a Navy ship, so--I was a Navy man, as was all the Seabees, which was a half of a battalion, and it was the 17th Naval Construction Battalion. So we had better quarters. I felt so sorry for those soldiers, because we were attached to the Eighth Army, basically, down in them dumb holes. Oh, God. What a way to be. Anyway, we had no more than got out of the harbor and the commander come on and he said, "I just want to notify all of you people that we are now at what they call submarine junction." I put on my life jacket and wore it for 18 days. I don't swim well. So on the morning of the 18th of--of November, they hit the beaches of French Morocco, a little town of Fidella (ph), which is north of Casablanca. I was going in on the second wave. And now my luck had started to go my way. As we were about ready to get over the side into the landing craft, the commander come on and said, "At ease, everybody." You know what that means in the Navy, at ease. The beaches are secure. So we didn't hit the beaches. We were kind of laying at anchor. And--and then the next morning we went into the Port of Casablanca. The French and the Germans had scuttled every ship in there. So there were only a couple of dock spaces available and there--we were tied up like this, you know. There was, I think, four ships side by side because--and our--our men in the--in our Seabee organization that were--that were into the--the divers and everything, they started immediately patching the holes and pumping the water out of these babies. And what they did with most of them is just--just haul them out--out and anchor them out of the harbor. And--but the crew that I was--I was a carpenter, and I met up with another young man from--from South Dakota that had the same exact background as I did, and a young man from Fremont, Ohio, that had a similar background. And our first job--first big job--we had a lot of little jobs. But the first big job was we took over all the warehouses on the--it would be on the east side of the Port of Casablanca. A lot of warehouses. And we started in there and we--we made an area where the plumbers in that started putting in showers and bathrooms. And my buddy and I, we--we started cleaning out the camel manure and putting in new concrete floors. And we put new concrete--holy. That time in the Navy, when you went into a place like that, if you needed a truck or you needed something, you just went and took it, you know. We--there wasn't any monkey business. Somehow or other they got a two-sack cement mixer, some--lots of sands, of course, because of the beaches, and some grout. And there was--we had some concrete finishers. And we started--my buddy and I, we put the screens in and got the levels and all of that stuff. And somewhere they found an old beatup transit for leveling. And that was our first big project. We worked on that for about two weeks, putting new floors in and--and at that time we didn't realize what we were doing, but we were building the Naval operating base for the Mediterranean Theater. And the Eighth Army, of course, who we were working with, they were--they were trying to run Rommel out of--out of North Africa and--and shut off the oil supply coming through North Africa to Hitler across the Mediterranean. Do you follow me?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: So then--after we got that done, then--I forgot to tell you. I was also assigned to guard duty at the--we had guards all around the port area. And we had only one problem after we got in there, and that was sniper fire. We were very careful what we did because we still had a few crazy Frenchmen and a few of the Germans that hadn't sneaked out yet still around trying to create some problems. But eventually, in about--about three or four weeks, we got things pretty well organized and then--then went to work on the--on the basics. And here's what I did while I was over there. I'm not looking for that in here. I'm just... I repaired roads in the city. And I--I repaired the runways at the airport at Casa. I repaired the hangars. Then I built quansa huts, tent cities, ammunition dumps. I did everything that--to prepare for the--what turned out to be a big influx of Army personnel coming through. And--it was interesting work. The bad side: The 17th Battalion was one of the first groups of Seabees. They only started in the--early in '42, you know. In this world we live in, it ain't what you know, it's who you know. The people I worked for, I wouldn't have hired a one of them. Until--I had been there about a year and we got a new lieutenant, took over our--our section of this thing. And he called my buddy from South Dakota and I to the side one morning. And he said, "Now look"--this guy was--name was Braky (ph), and I'm Painter. He said, "I want to tell you guys something. I'm from the oil fields of Texas. I don't know a damn thing about the building business." He says, "I'll get your morning orders and I'll turn you guys lose and you do what has to be done." Treated us like a million bucks. The only good officer I ran into. He--in the morning, he wold come down and he would say--he would bring a sheet of paper this big, passes. He would give us eight passes a piece. He said, "When you get your work done, if you want to go to town a little." Braky was a married guy and so was I, so we didn't do any running around. We--when--if I had any spare time, I was--I worked with the chaplains. They needed shelves, they needed this. And I--I would help them dig up the stuff they needed, and so would Braky. And then we started getting on top of things. I saw many accidents where people got killed. One evening, an experienced--this don't mean anything. Experience--one evening I was getting--sitting by my bunk and--because most of the time we worked day and night, you know, depending on what we needed to do. And in comes a chaplain. And he says, "Painter," he says, "I need a little help." I said, "Okay." You know, we never went outside without our cover. We call it cover. Without your cap or--but we wore helmets over there. And went outside. There was another gentleman there that's from the--from the--from the Army. And we started walking down the dock to the--to the south. And I thought, 'What in the heck is going on here?' We got down there and we--this guy from the Army, he said, "Here it is, right here." We looked over to the side. Here was a body floating around, and he wanted me to help him get it out of the water. Do you know what happens after a body has been in the water a while? Well, we tried to get the identification of this guy before we--we put what do you call its under them to pick him up. Took his ring off and his whole damn finger come off. It's--it's a tough life for an old country boy from Chesterland, Ohio. Anyway, we got that job done. And then I then was shipped from--from the Casablanca area, which was my basic headquarters, to a little town of Agadir. Tore down a base there and turned it over to the French, with a runway. I did the same at a little town of Safi, father south. Took ammunition dumps that had been buried, you know, dug them out, took them all apart, loaded them on boxcars and shipped them up north. And after we had finished that trip, we--there was only an officer and two of us guys and a truck driver. We were in a--in the morning, we started to go from there back to Casablanca. It was grasshopper time. For two days the grasshoppers were so thick, you couldn't see the sun. But we were traveling all the time. It was like--it was like driving over popcorn. And we got back in to Casa and we immediately got our orders to go up to what was at that time the--the--the Naval Air Operation and a place called Port Lyautey. We went up there, and we were there for a couple of weeks. And I was just helping build quansa huts and that type of stuff. And then they loaded us all on these--what do they call them? 40 in 8 boxcars? You know, 40 men or eight horses. And they shipped us to Azrou, a two-day ride. Rained all the way. The roof leaked. There was--us guys were in there. We didn't do any sleeping. We were in groups underneath our ponchos trying to keep dry, you know. What a deal. Anyway, we got to Azrou and we went right aboard ship. And the next morning we took off and went out. We went through the Strait of Gibralter. And boy, when we got out there, I couldn't believe what I was seeing. There were ships everywhere. Do you know what the date was? It was June the 5th. June--they were going to invade that day but because of the weather, they put it off to the 6th. Now, we don't know where we're going and whether we're a part of this or not or whether we were going to England because--but that day, we--as we were traveling, I was positive we were going in a westerly direction. And sure enough, the next morning we were all by our self heading back to the States. So, came back to the States, had a little leave, went back to Davisville, Rhode Island, and worked on helping with the maintenance and everything. And then the greatest thing that ever happened in this world: Harry Truman knocked the hell out of the Japs. I was scheduled for the second wave to hit the mainland of Japan. So who do you think I think is the greatest president in the world? I'm here because of him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: And--so anyway, then--by the fact I had previous military time, when the--when the discharge setup came for getting out, I had more than enough points to be, so I was one of the first guys that came--I got back home on--on the first day of October, 1945. Now, while we were over there, other than on our convoy going across, there were ten ships, and we had ten--eight destroyers, or tin cans, that were guarding us. They circled us all the time. At night, if you were awake, all you could hear was them darn depth charges going off. You never were sure if they were really after a submarine or not. But that was them 42ing. You know, they were sinking four and five ships every day in the Atlantic. We were very fortunate. So, after we were over in Casa, we--we were hit by air raids. Bombers come over and dropping bombs around.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any close calls there?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Not--not for me. Because after we had been over there for about six months, the group I was in, we took over an old theater up in--in the city of Casablanca. And we took all the seats out. And that's--we moved in there. We never did have any hot water there for six months. If we wanted to take a shower, we had to go back down to the main base. And--but I--I didn't get my Purple Heart or--for--because I was out in an air raid. I was out where I shouldn't have been, instead of being in the air raid shelter, and I got clipped by a piece of shrapnel. I never reported it to anybody, because back in the old days, if you got something like that, you're more than liable to get a court marshal than you were to get any honor, I'll tell you. So anyway, then--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you did get a Purple Heart, you say?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I didn't. No. I didn't even report it. I never spent one day in the sick bay after we left the States. I had a little trouble with--with sinus before we left the States. But after I got in North Africa, never hit the sick bay at all. It was odd weather over there, you know, in the edge of the desert. You get up in the morning and it would be cold as heck. And we had these old-fashioned sheep skin coats. But by noontime you were in your shirt sleeves. It would warm up like crazy. But you get adjusted to all of that stuff, so... What else is exciting?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Oh, ho, ho, ho. Yes, yes, yes. Right now, I don't know if there's any of them still alive. I'm 88, and that's getting up there. There was a young fellow from Mayfield Heights by the name of Burt Shaw (ph). He passed away a few years ago. And I just see by the--the old--I also belong to the Seabee Reunion Group. And I see that his wife, Virginia, just passed way. Dick Tates (ph). We had not been back to the States too long and he passed away. He was a good friend. I have never--oh, I'm wrong. This Braky from South Dakota, him and I used to send Christmas cards. But I haven't heard from him and he hasn't heard from me for years. So I don't know if there are any of the--of my old gang still living or not. And I have a complete list of the--all the people that belong to the Arizona Reunion Group. And there was only one name on there that I could remember being--but see, I was in the Fourth Division, and there was 1100-and-some people, so you didn't know them all. I played--I played baseball regular. I played a little basketball when we're in Bremerton, Washington, in the Navy yard. Played football. In 1936, I played in the back field with a quarterback from the--from Annapolis that was one of the All Americans that year. Buzz Borey (ph). Did you ever hear that name?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It sounds familiar.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Buzz Borey.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: He wasn't a very big guy, but God, was he tough. Woo. We had--we had a mediocre football team we played. We played Woodbury College; and baseball, we played Stanford University. I was in--in the sand lots of San Francisco in the early '30s. Do you know who was--it was a group of young guys there. We were practicing and they'd come over and they said, "How would you guys like to have a ball game?" And, of course, our manager was--was a JG, you know. He said, "Sure." So we played these young guys. And none of them signed their name except Don, Joe, this, whatever. Do you know who they were? The Di Maggio brothers and the Disotells (ph) and them all guys, all become major league ball players. They whomped the heck out of us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'll bet.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Oh, God. Oh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you played against Joe Di Maggio, huh?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Evidently, yeah. You know, it's a great life. It's a great life. I've--I've had more than my share of good breaks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were any of your buddies still on the Arizona when it was attacked?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I have been out to the memorial twice. Not too many of them that I really knew well. Not too many of them. If I would have been aboard that, I would have had a good chance of surviving because the bomb went in up in front of the--the forward mast, right down into the--to the--the magazines are down in the bottom. And I was in the Fourth Division, which would have been back towards the--I call it the quarterdeck. Back towards the end. That area was not damaged as much as the other areas. Now, the problem would have been getting through the water and the burning oil. Bad. But, thank God I wasn't there. So I was going to tell you my dog tag number that I got in 1933 is 2830844.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you had it written down. You still could have remembered it?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I only wrote it in here because, see, my memory is--is beginning to really slip.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You're doing great.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I used to be able to spit that out. My Social Security number, my wife's Social Security number, and this. But--and I'm--I'm a life member in American Legion Post 459 in Burton, Ohio. I'm a life member in the 6519 VFW post over here. And I just got hooked up with this Seabee outfit in Cleveland, called 9X or something. They have a monthly meeting down at the--at the, ah, Coast Guard station on Ninth Street. They have a monthly meeting down there. And through the--through my friendship at the Senior Center here, I have met up with--with a Seabee that lives in Novelty, Ohio, and he's now joined up with this group. And he still drives at night and I don't. And we're going to start taking in their meetings. They meet the third Tuesday of every month. And they've got a Christmas party coming up, and we're intending to get in that. And love to get with these old guys and listen to their stories. Now, the Seabee that I'm friendly with, he didn't get in until about three years after I did. So he was in the South Pacific. And from what I know about the South Pacific, I got the best deal.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you Stateside, then, when the war ended? You were still in the States when they dropped the bombs and the war ended?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Here, yes. I had come back from--from French Morocco and was in the States waiting to be--to go out again. My--my schedule was January 1946.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were going to invade the mainland?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: They were going to hit--I was the second wave hitting the mainland in Japan. And you know, if that would had ever happened, it would have been a horrible slaughter. Those people were very dedicated, and they--and--I'm sure you know that so many of these people, they have so much underground living stuff. Oh, man. We could get Hussein, maybe. But he's--he lives underground. They know where you're going to bomb him under there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Overseas?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Well, one of the experiences that I remember real well is when they were bombing the hell out of us and I went where I shouldn't have been and they--and the--they put the flares up, you know. Have you ever--anybody ever told you about flares? Well, my God. You feel safe if you're hiding behind a twig. Oh, man. That was--that was really something. Then I got hit by the shrapnel, so I had to get the heck out of there. Yeah, I remember that real well.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Shrapnel from a bomb?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Yep. It was probably our own. No, I think it was more shrapnel from our own aircraft batteries because they were--and that's funny, that night. I woke up and I could hear this rumble, and they kept getting closer and closer. And I thought, 'What the heck is going on?' This is one particular time. And it kept getting closer and closer. And then, all of a sudden, it come to me, there's--our aircraft batteries along the coast of French Morocco, they're banging away at the German aircraft that's coming this way. It kept getting closer and closer and closer. A string of bombs hit the port area that--where I told you we put all that concrete in. And we had air-raid shelters. And there was a piece of a bomb that big a-round, came through the roof of that thing, right through a guy's bunk. But he was where he belonged, in the air-raid shelter. Their bombing was not too accurate. They hit--they hit out by the airport. Another string of bombs hit a highway about halfway between the city of Casa and the airport. The airport was out a little bit. I had the good fortunate of going out and repairing the road and all of that stuff. But there was--it was interesting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, when you were on guard duty, did you have any close encounters with snipers?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Lucked out?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: No. No. I had only one bad experience, and if they had caught me, I would have got a court marshal. About the fourth time I went on guard duty--and we would be out only four hours. We're-Seabees are noncombat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: But somebody had to do this job. As they--let's see. And this is the part of the military I don't like. The--the guy in charge said, "No live ammunition today." One of the guys on the--on the watch ahead of me told me about it. Clip of shells down in my sock. The minute I got on post, clip of shells in my--I had an '03. You know, we didn't have the newest stuff. We had the Springfield '03 .30-06s. And I put that baby right in there. And if they would have caught me, they would have probably court marshaled me. But see, I see these--where these terrorists have hit these camps and killed a lot of people. The guards can't do nothing. They don't have any ammunition. You know, this has been typical of our military to do that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Are they afraid you'll accidentally shoot somebody?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I don't understand it. I don't understand it. Of course, the difference between myself and a lot of the people I run into was I was born and raised with a gun. When I was seven years old, under the Christmas tree was a little 22 rifle. You'll get this one. Boy, I started under that Christmas tree. Dad said, "Don't touch that gun." He said, "After breakfast we'll go out behind the barn"--we lived on a little farm. "We'll go out behind the barn." And he says, "I'll teach you how to use that rifle." And the first thing he said to me--I remember it like yesterday. He says, "You don't point this thing at anything you don't want to kill." And it was a little 22. It only shot shorts. But from then on, I was--I was out shooting rabbits and squirrels. That's what we ate those days. Life was tough. That's kind of where I've been. I-- END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE:

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you--the guys--when you were overseas, did you do anything for entertainment, anything to--

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Oh. The Merchant Marine and the Liberty Ships. They started bringing in--in movies. And they--we had a movie camera and we put a big screen up in the--in our dining room. And they had--they had a movie about--I think four nights a week that we could go. I'm not a movie buff, but I went to a few of them because what else was there to do in the evening after--I didn't work every night. As it turned out--you see, we were the Naval operating base for the Mediterranean Theater. And as we got towards the end of my enlistment, I was up in--in the--in the city of Casablanca, working nights. After the officers would get through with their day, then their offices, we would go in and do remodeling and all of that stuff. And I can tell you this now, I had to take--I had to take a--let's see. Stuff bothers me. Anyway, I took a pledge. We went into a big room and they had put sheet metal on the walls. And they had the--all of the oceans and every ship--they used them little magnets, you know. Every ship--German, American, French, English--was marked on that. And I did the maintenance in there. But when I walked out of there, I never said a word. If I did, I got in trouble. Do you follow me?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Yeah. I had some--you see, I look at it--I wasn't happy with the way--the way it was because of our leadership. But on the other hand, I had some good experiences. We--this friend of mine, Braky, and I, we--there was a Liberty Ship come in that had taken a torpedo, and it had a big hole in the side. So that our welders went down and put the--a temporary patch over it. My buddy and I, we went in and we formed inside of that 40 feet long and about 12 feet high, and put in all reinforcing rod and we poured concrete behind the patch so they could bring the ship back to the United States. Now, then, my buddy and I, we--we did the whole layout, everything. We had to make a hopper to get the concrete in there. And they--and they had some soldiers and some sailors. They worked four-hour shifts mixing concrete for a day and a half. Never stopped. My buddy and I, we were there the complete time, because that was our project, you know, and shipped that old baby back. And then, a little later on, there was one of these little PBYs come in, had taken a torpedo and had--and they cut this thing apart and it took one of the engine rooms out. They operate on two big 12-cylinder jobs. And they got this all done. And nobody that they had had the talent to line up the engine with the drive shafts because they wanted to put in a new base, you know, put the engine on. So who do you think got the call? My buddy and I. We went over and we told them what we thought we needed in equipment. We finally got it. And we got that baby. In about four days they had all the welding done and they put the 12-cylinder engine that they had and they sent that baby back to the States. Experiences. In the harbor of Casablanca was the new French battleship called the Jean Bart. It never--never went out to sea at all. They had not completely finished it. It hadn't been commissioned. But it sit there in the harbor all the time. And then, a little later on, you know, they had Degal and Roosevelt and everybody had a big meeting in Casablanca. And all I did in that, when they were over there, was stand a little guard. And see, we--our particular group moved into this theater uptown. And under the canopy out in the front in the morning when we would go out, there would be anywhere from 15 to 50 little Arab kids all piled up there in a bunch, sleeping, just like animals. It was nothing to see a little Arab dead on the street. But--then we would have to walk from there to the main base to get our chow. We would get up in the morning, get ready to go, walk down, get our chow. We would get our--we would be all set to go. After we eat, we would go out, we would get our orders for the day. And somewhere along the line, they got a--a ton and a half dump truck that was our baby. And we had our truck driver. Took us where we had to go, got all of our material for us. It was interesting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with the people over there okay, though, the civilians?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I had taken French in--in high school. And I could understand more than I could talk. And most of the people in the--well, in the taverns--and we didn't go in many stores-- they would talk French. So I got along okay with them. But my problem was with the Arabs. Couldn't trust them. They're no different now than they were then. Can't trust the Arabs. And, of course, they've got that one guy they're trying right now from French Morocco. This terrorist setup that we have is a big organization. We haven't begun to see what's going to happen in that yet, my opinion. I've been there. I'm using my experience as my guide a little bit. So...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Seabees were civilians that were paid by the government?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We were--we were a member --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Abide by all the rules of the--

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We were under the control of the Navy, and we were just construction people. My outfit, the 17th, there were--they sent us a half a battalion to Greenland and a half a battalion I was--we went with the invasion of North Africa. I was 28 years old when I hit the beach, and the oldest guy in our outfit, all volunteers, was 48 years old. We had the best damn mechanics in the world. We could do anything, just give us a little time. I--I appreciated the people I worked with. I mean, the workers, not the--not the leaders. Whew.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there a set term of enlistment, or were you there as long as they needed you or--

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We were just the same as being in the regular Navy. When the--when the war was over and they come out with a discharge form that--which was by points, that's the way we got put out. And by my previous service, I was one of the first ones out. Some of these guys had only been in the Seabees for a couple of years, they were the last ones to get out. And--but it was--I have good memories. I was happy to get home. Got back to--I lived in Chesterland, and we had built a new house and I didn't have it finished. So from October until after the first of January I didn't do anything but work at home, finishing--I did all--I'm an Englishman, and I did all the stone work, which is this haphazard pattern of sand stone, you know. And I--and I finally built the stairs going from the main floor to the second floor, which I had a big dormer. I had two bedrooms and a bath.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories when you first got home, your reunion with your wife?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Oh, yeah. My--my good wife. Yes. I was very happy to be back with her because she's been my guiding light for 65 years. Nope, I can't say enough good things about my queen. If I talk Navy language, will you understand it? Do you know where the quarterdeck is?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No. Back here?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Stern.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: And you can see the Number Two Catapult right there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: That picture was taken right after 1934, because the crane on the stern was brand-new in 1934. And that was my baby.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were right there under that second catapult, this one?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: This one here is the one. Right here. Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That one, okay.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: That's on the top of Number Three Turret. Number Four Turret is right there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: After I get the planes in the air, then I went in--for general quarters, I went in there and I--and I could go underneath between the deck and the bottom of the turret. And there was a little hatch there this big, that I could crawl up in it to get up to my battle station. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Your battle station was in the turret, then?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Yeah, up in the upper chambers. And I think I told you, I was trained to relieve everybody that was involved.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This ship was built, what? About nineteen--

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Sixteen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: 1916. All right.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Yep. Two years after I was born. The aircraft the Macon, just before she went down, we--we were in the Battleship Arizona. In our six battleships we were in the --in the group that tried to find survivors from that, if you remember that day.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I do remember that. Great pictures?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Here I am with the old--our aircraft were bi-planes. They were--they were Voughts. They were strictly for observation off of battleships. And we used to shoot them off and then we would pick them up on a sea sled with a crane. And here's the old baby in the dry dock. Now, aboard the old battleship, we had 14-inch--four turrets, 14 inch. Then we had our--our aircraft/antiaircraft batteries. They were five-inch antiaircraft. And then we have the five-inch broadsides. Which this guy here is--this is one of the antiaircraft. Are you old enough to remember a movie that was made years and years ago, called "Here Comes the Navy"?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I think I've seen it. Yes.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Who do you recognize there?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's see here. James Cagney?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: James Cagney. Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Frank McHugh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Frank McHugh, okay.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Gloria Stuart and Joan Blondell.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In this picture you've got Pat O'Brien, James Cagney. And...

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: So--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's great. So you took the snapshot?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it was shot on the Arizona?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Part of it?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I didn't realize that.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Yeah. That was done nineteen--I went aboard in July of 1933. And I'm not sure, but they didn't do it that fall.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I saw this movie maybe six months ago.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: There's another thing I forgot to mention to you that's kind of off the subject a little bit. But, we went overseas a half a battalion. About six months later they sent a half a battalion to join us. We become--from the 17th, we become the 120th. And these people were all from New York and New Jersey. Does that tell you anything?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: They're completely different than the Midwesterners. When--when we went in to camp, there was Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Illinois. I think that's it. If I wanted to take a shower, I could leave my billfold laying on my bunk. When that gang from the east joined us, they stole everything. That was a different bunch of people. And I--I had a heck of a time understanding that. I didn't realize that there was that much difference in it. They were raised different. I even--there were even guys came in there that had never driven a car. They were raised in the big city of New York or New Jersey or somewhere down there. It's hard to understand. When I got out of the Navy in 1933, I could have went and had a tryout with the Coast League in California. But it was different then. I had to--I had to rent my own motel and pay my own bill. Today, they give you all of that stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: And I didn't have any money. So--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you couldn't afford to do the tryout?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: So I didn't take a shot at it. I had a pitcher, two--one--one pitcher from our team and one pitcher from another team and a couple of--of the--of the guys that played with me, not necessarily on my team, tried out for the Coast League. Our big right-hander, his name was Tobin. He got into professional baseball but he never got any higher than the Coast League out there. Never made it to the majors.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Coast League was a pretty big deal, though,back there --

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: --before major league baseball moved into the West Coast?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: You know, my friend just died.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you know him?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: Mel Harder?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: If you go look in my desk, you'll see Mel and I in a nice picture in there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I didn't know him real well. A very good friend of mine and he played a lot of golf together, and that's how I got to know him, playing golf with him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: And then he used to sponsor the cancer thing and always went with that. And he was--he was a real gentleman.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: And, you know, they talk about, well, this guy's going to be--what do they call them now? In the hall of fame, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: And they talk about Alamar (ph). And I said what are they talking about? This is all politics. Here's one of the greatest pitchers that ever come along. Mel Harder, and he can't make it. You know why? Because he wouldn't--he wouldn't talk to the sports writers like the other guys.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: See, this--it's --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, they have that list in the paper of all these guys who have won less games than him that are in the hall of fame. He won about 223 games or something?

sp.speaker: Eugene R. Painter
sp.p: I had the good fortunate of seeing the Babe Ruth play when I was a little bitty guy. My dad took me to League Park. The Babe was there playing. I can't remember who in the heck pitched that game. I think Babe--that day, I think the first time up he hit a homerun. And I was only about six or seven years old. And I saw Mel pitch quite a bit because I used to go to a lot of games.
